title: Lester's showmanship: playing the tenor upside down and behind his back
summary: Phillips describes Lester's Tiger Rag trick of playing with the mouthpiece turned and a hand behind his back, begun in Minneapolis, and his skating and Charleston on the carnival.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: How long solos did he get? How many choruses?
When he played "Tiger Rag," about ten. He had an act he did, too, you know.
Tell me about that.
He used to take his mouthpiece off the horn and turn it around, and play it like he was smoking a pipe. You see what I mean?
Phillips - 114
I see. Playing the horn upside-down. Up in the air.
Yeah.
With the bell pointing straight down to the floor, playing the tenor like that.
Yeah, the tenor like that.
Turned the mouthpiece upside-down so the bottom of the reed would still be on his lip.
Yeah. But the horn was up. He played that, and he took breaks. [SINGS] He'd do that when it was up like that. Then he'd take it and play it this way, put his hands around it -- play it like that.
They can't see that, so describe it.
He would take the horn like this, hands here, place (?) being here; he'd take it around here and play it.
He'd put a hand behind his back...
[END OF TAPE 2, SIDE 4]

When the tape went off, you were talking about how Lester would put his left hand behind his back and he would finger the bottom of the tenor saxophone, and his right hand would be in the front, fingering with the top hand. That's one of the tricks he did with King Oliver.
He did that with all of them, at the time.
Phillips - 115
But he quit putting a floor show on. He said he'd just play now. He said he don't have to put no floor show on to play.
Right. But he did those things...
Then.
Right. But he did them in the 20's, too. Or just with King Oliver?
Yeah, he did it in the 20's. He used to dance and play. He used to do the Charleston and play.
He did that with King Oliver, too?

No. He did that on the carnival. He used to skate and play. They had a dance called Skate, and they used to do that -- skate all over. [SINGS 'YESSIR, THAT'S MY BABY' AND PREZ' IMPROVISATION] See, he could dance good, you know. He was a good dancer.
Let's touch on that a little more. He did a lot of his showmanship with the carnival show, and he'd dance while playing.
Yeah. I mean, that was on the show, but he didn't do much... Not with his horn. He didn't do too much showmanship with his horn on the carnival. He just played.
When did he do most of his showmanship on...? Oh, you mean when he did the Skate and when he did the Charleston. That was without the horn.
Yeah, he had the horn. That was on the carnival.
Phillips - 116
Okay. On the carnival show, he had to do the Skate and the Charleston when he was playing the horn.
Yeah. But this other thing, turn it up and put behind it like that, he did that while he was playing in he band.
When did he start that? With Willis Young's dance band?
Yeah, that's when he started. It started out in Minneapolis. Because he saw...
Did anybody else do that, or did he just pick it up on his own?

No. Yeah, he saw a cat somewhere, I'm trying to see who he was, playing the horn, like I said, with the left hand behind him. Whenever we played "Tiger Rag," we'd feature him. See, that was his number, "Tiger Rag." And we played it way up in tempo too. He'd play it this way and make all the breaks up this way, then after we'd get down to the trio part and go back in the chorus again, he put it behind him and made the breaks behind him, then when we'd get through he'd make a cadenza on the end with it behind him, and then come on out. He'd great the house up. I mean, the house went down everywhere that he did that. Because you didn't see nobody doin' nothin' like that.
No, I guess not. So he was doing that with King Oliver, too.
Yeah. He did with the Blue Devils and
Phillips - 117
everybody he played with.
